book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy

chapters.file: ch67 - 63. Amy Schumer as Philosopher Fuck the Feminine Mystique.md
chapters.relation: Elsby argues Amy Schumer's honest comedy revolts against a 'feminine mystique' broader than Friedan's housewife version, running back to Beauvoir's claim that woman is constructed as the 'Other' and to Aristotle's 'rational animal' definition that cast women as irrational and thus less than human. Through bits like 'Madame President,' 'Last Fuckable Day,' the 'New Twitter Button' sketch, and gross-out honesty about pregnancy and her own body in Growing and The Leather Special, Schumer refuses to let women's physical, sexual, and social experience stay mysterious. Elsby reads this as de-'othering' and re-humanizing women by forcing our concept of 'woman' to expand to include flawed, fully human hot-mess figures.

chapters.file: ch68 - 64. George Carlin as Philosopher It’s All Bullshit. Is It Bad for Ya.md
chapters.relation: Engels reads Carlin's insistence that 'it's all bullshit, and it's bad for ya' as a defense of truth over comforting illusion, mapping his bits onto Plato's Allegory of the Cave (Carlin dragging audiences up from shadows like 'prostitution is immoral' or 'the American Dream' to expose deeper essences), Nozick's Experience Machine (Carlin's sun-worship chosen because it is real, not a pleasing fiction), and Clifford/Beauvoir on the ethics of belief and the 'serious world.' Bits on rights, the sanctity of life, homelessness/'houselessness,' and 'proud to be an American' show Carlin arguing that false beliefs breed complacency and harm, so there are moral reasons to prefer truth.

chapters.file: ch69 - 65. Louis CK as Philosopher The King and His Fall.md
chapters.relation: Marra Henrigillis first shows CK as 'philosopher king of comedy'—his cell-phone/'forever empty' bit echoing Buddhist and Stoic teaching on sitting with suffering, his 'why?' bit echoing Quine on not ontologizing, his 'So Did The Fat Lady' episode exposing how society denies fat women full humanity—then uses his 2017 misconduct scandal to stage competing verdicts: the feminist case for banning him (rape culture, power dynamics), Plato on censoring vicious art, Mill's four-part defense of free expression and Nozick's free-market/entitlement view against cancellation, and Aristotle's virtue ethics (character judged over a whole life) plus Pompa's prison-education view that no one is only their worst act.

chapters.file: ch70 - 66. Marc Maron as Philosopher Comedy, Therapy, and Identification.md
chapters.relation: Kapica argues Maron's 'WTF' philosophy—both indignation and liberation—turns Kenneth Burke's rhetorical theory of identification and 'consubstantiality' into comedic catharsis, treating stand-up as therapy. He reads Maron's opening move from 'What is the meaning of life?' to 'How am I being used?' through Richard Taylor and Camus's Sisyphus: in 2009, a broke and failing Maron is Sisyphus, and WTF is his license to invent meaning. Via his cold-sore and sobriety bits and his WTF podcast interviews (Seinfeld, Gallagher), Maron makes his audience a surrogate therapist, using performed vulnerability to bind them into an 'acting-together' that Kapica claims genuinely saved Maron's life.

chapters.file: ch71 - 67. Hari Kondabolu as Philosopher Enacting a Philosophy of Liberation.md
chapters.relation: Heppard frames Kondabolu—who resists the 'political comic' label—as enacting Enrique Dussel's 'philosophy of liberation' and Marcuse's aesthetics of liberation: comedy as 'barbarian philosophy' spoken from the periphery. Kondabolu's Swiftian 'eat the rich' health-care proposal, his 'White Chocolate Joke,' 'Feminist Dick Joke,' Columbus/Joe DiMaggio bit, and Bobby Jindal takedown rupture the audience's identification with white supremacy, patriarchy, and liberal hypocrisy (negative freedom) while his absurd alternatives exercise the 'radical imagination' (positive freedom). Heppard concludes that although comedians are not revolutionaries, the revolution must be funny.

chapters.file: ch72 - 68. Richard Pryor as Philosopher Stand-Up Comedy and Gramsci’s Organic Intellectual.md
chapters.relation: Healy reads Pryor through Gramsci's Prison Notebooks concept of the 'organic intellectual'—someone who gains specialized knowledge through lived experience and uses it to challenge a capitalist/racist hegemony—arguing Pryor's mainstream white fame let him smuggle the Black experience to the dominant class. Analyzing his concert films (Live in Concert, Live on the Sunset Strip, Here and Now), Healy shows Pryor's chokehold and police-dog bits, the 'Yee Haw'/lynching bit, and the Mudbone and Motif characters using laughter as a 'Trojan Horse' to make white audiences absorb police brutality, the Great Migration, and heroin death—Pryor as philosophy in action.

chapters.file: ch73 - 69. Larry David as Philosopher Interrogating Convention.md
chapters.relation: Carroll treats Curb Your Enthusiasm as a Kantian/Marxian 'critique'—an inquiry into the conditions of possibility—of everyday norms of civility, built on incongruity humor and Mary Douglas's theory of jokes as 'anti-rites.' Through episodes like the handicapped-stutterer, the new-house tour Larry refuses, the phone-call cutoff time, Ben Stiller's no-gifts party, and the buried five-wood, David shows that manners are non-necessary and arbitrary yet held in place only by intense (uncurbed) emotional 'enthusiasm,' epitomized by Susie Greene's operatic rage. Carroll answers the analytic skeptic by casting David's method as Socratic/maieutic (like Plato's Meno): the argument is completed in the reflective viewer's mind.

holes.name: Identification and Consubstantiality
holes.what: Kenneth Burke's rhetorical theory that persuasion works by making a speaker 'consubstantial' with the audience through shared symbols, bridging division into an 'acting-together.'
holes.why: Chapter 70 makes Burke's identification/consubstantiality and 'comic frame' the entire theoretical spine of its account of Maron's comedy-as-therapy, and the taxonomy has no philosopher or concept covering Burke or rhetorical identification.

holes.name: Enrique Dussel
holes.what: Latin-American philosopher and founder of the philosophy of liberation, which theorizes thinking from the 'exteriority' of the oppressed periphery rather than the European center.
holes.why: Chapter 71 builds its central argument on Dussel's Philosophy of Liberation (barbarian philosophy, otherness, exteriority) alongside Marcuse, and the taxonomy contains no philosopher of liberation for the periphery.

holes.name: The Organic Intellectual
holes.what: Gramsci's figure who gains knowledge through the lived experience of a subaltern class and uses it to articulate that class's interests and challenge ruling-class hegemony.
holes.why: Chapter 72's whole thesis is that Pryor IS an organic intellectual; the taxonomy lists Gramsci only via 'hegemony,' with no slug for the organic-intellectual concept the chapter applies throughout.
